# Writing skills for this kit

The repository ships one canonical format: an [Agent Skills](https://agentskills.io) folder per workflow. Hosts differ in paths and invocation, never in content.

## File shape

```
skills/<name>/
└── SKILL.md
```

Optional supporting files are allowed (`references/`, `scripts/`, `assets/`) but must be referenced from `SKILL.md`, because hosts only load what the body points at.

## Frontmatter

```yaml
---
name: audit-next
description: One sentence on what it does, then exactly when to use it. Front-load trigger words; hosts truncate long lists.
---
```

Enforced by `npm test`:

| Rule | Reason |
| :--- | :--- |
| `name` equals the folder name | Copilot silently drops skills whose name does not match its folder |
| lowercase, digits, hyphens, max 64 chars | Slash-command grammars in every host |
| `description` under 1,024 chars | Host-side truncation limit |
| no `$ARGUMENTS`, `$1` … | Only two hosts substitute them; the rest would show the literal token |
| no `subagent`, `model`, `allowed-tools` | Host-specific fields that other hosts ignore or reject |
| LF endings, no absolute paths | Windows checkouts and portable installs |

## Body contract

1. **Say what to do, not why the skill exists.** Rationale belongs in the README.
2. **Declare an `## Arguments` section in prose.** The text after the command is the input; state what happens when it is empty.
3. **State the output contract.** How long the chat reply is, and which file holds the detail.
4. **Make evidence mandatory.** If a step claims a defect, the body must demand a reproduction that fails first.
5. **Guard destructive steps.** Require an explicit confirmation token before deleting or committing.
6. **Stay host-neutral.** No pronouns for the tool, no "ask the user to click", no assumptions about model choice.
7. **Keep the body under ~120 lines.** Every host pays for it in context; long skills get summarised and lose constraints.

## Anti-patterns rejected in review

- A skill that only restates "review the code carefully".
- A checklist with no verification step, so the agent can claim a finding without evidence.
- Instructions that depend on a previous conversation turn.
- Duplicated skill content: if two skills share rules, extract them into the body of each (hosts do not compose skills) or accept the duplication deliberately and keep it identical.
- Personal defaults (language, tone, comment style) baked in as universal requirements.

## Testing a change

```bash
npm test
node bin/cli.mjs install --dry-run
node bin/cli.mjs install --skills <name> --link
```

With `--link`, edits in this repository are live in your agent, so you can iterate without reinstalling.

name: audit-final
description: Synthesize a completed codebase audit into FINAL_AUDIT_REPORT.md. Aggregates module findings, audits cross-module boundaries (wire contracts, state desync, layering, trust boundaries), runs the global test baseline, and produces a severity-ordered bug table, roadmap, and PR plan. Use when every module is audited and audit_state.json reports SYNTHESIS_READY.
---

# Audit synthesis

You are the Principal Systems Architect running the final pass. Verified findings live in `.tmp/audit/findings/*.md`.

## Arguments

If the text after the command contains `no-pr-plan`, skip section 8 of the report. Otherwise ignore it.

## Rules

1. **Verified only.** A bug enters the master table only if its reproduction was run and failed against HEAD. `UNVERIFIED` observations go into a separate appendix.
2. Every row carries a `file:line` anchor and the exact reproduction command.
3. Chat output under 15 lines; all detail goes to the report.
4. Reply in the user's language; report body in English.
5. State the audit coverage (modules audited versus discovered) in the report header. A partial audit is still a result, but it must be visible.

## Steps

### 1. Ingest

- Read every `.tmp/audit/findings/*.md` and `.tmp/audit/audit_state.json`.
- Confirm no module was skipped; if one was, say so explicitly.
- Run each domain's full test suite and static analyzer to capture a global baseline: total tests, passing/failing, analyzer status, duration.

### 2. Cross-module and boundary review

Audit the seams isolation cannot see. One finding per real defect, prefixed `X1`, `X2`, ...:

- **Wire and schema contracts.** Compare API or schema contracts (REST, GraphQL, gRPC/Protobuf, JSON schema) against persistence models and client types. Look for case-sensitivity mismatches, unmapped enum values, nullability drift, and silent field drops on round-trip.
- **State and concurrency desynchronisation.** When a transition happens in one module (sign-out, permission revocation, tier change, cache invalidation), do downstream modules and in-flight workers invalidate deterministically?
- **Layering and dependency inversion.** Do core or storage packages import transport, presentation, or UI layers?
- **Security and trust boundaries.** Are authorization claims, tenant boundaries, or rate-limit identities taken from unverified client input instead of authoritative server state?

### 3. Write `FINAL_AUDIT_REPORT.md` at the project root

1. **Executive summary and stack overview**: architectural health, domains and runtimes, headline verified risks, audit coverage.
2. **Subsystem and feature catalog**: directory breakdown by domain plus an ASCII dependency graph.
3. **Cross-boundary review**: the `X*` findings.
4. **Master critical bugs table** (`F1`, `F2`, ...) ordered by severity:
   - **Critical**: data corruption, wire deserialisation drops, phantom state mutations, active security or tenant bypass, loss of paid entitlements.
   - **High**: deterministic races, unhandled crash paths, cross-user state leaks, silent error swallowing.
   - **Medium**: unbounded memory growth, sub-optimal retry or caching, unpruned collections.
   Each row: root cause, `file:line`, reproduction command, minimal unified diff.
5. **Algorithmic and scalability bottlenecks**: multi-scale benchmark tables, Big-O, proposed replacement.
6. **Phased roadmap**: Phase 1 (Critical and High, fix now) covers correctness, wire drops, and isolation. Phase 2 (Medium, backlog) covers algorithms, pruning, and test blind spots.
7. **What not to change**: three to five pragmatic decisions that work and must be preserved to avoid needless risk.
8. **PR plan** (unless skipped): group fixes into reviewable units, one PR per module or per cross-boundary cluster, each with a Conventional Commits title, the finding IDs it closes, the test files it touches, and its dependencies on other PRs. Order by severity, then by merge risk.
9. **Appendix: UNVERIFIED**: findings without a reproduction, and why.

### 4. Close the phase

- Set `"status": "COMPLETED"` in `.tmp/audit/audit_state.json`.
- Do not delete `.tmp/audit/findings/`: the remediation commands read the root causes from there.
- Print both cleanup commands for later:

```bash
rm -rf .tmp/audit
```

```powershell
Remove-Item -Recurse -Force .tmp/audit
```

## Output

1. Report path, verified counts by severity, `X*` count.
2. Top three headline risks, one line each.
3. PR plan: number of PRs and the first one.
4. State `COMPLETED` and the next action: `fix-init`.

name: audit-init
description: Bootstrap an iterative, multi-stage codebase audit. Detects the stack from manifests, partitions the repository into cohesive modules (5-20 files each), resolves the exact test command per module, and writes .tmp/audit/audit_state.json. Use when starting a full architecture or correctness audit of a repo, when asked to review an entire codebase, or when the audit state file does not exist yet.
---

# Audit initialization

You are a Principal Software Architect initializing an iterative audit. This turn inspects the workspace, partitions it into audit modules, resolves tooling, and initializes state on disk.

**Do not audit code in this turn.**

## Arguments

The text after the command is the audit scope:

- empty: audit the whole repository in the current working directory;
- a path (for example `packages/api`): restrict the audit to that subtree.

## Rules

1. **Portability.** Never assume a language, framework, or layout. Detect the stack from manifests: `package.json`, `pubspec.yaml`, `go.mod`, `Cargo.toml`, `pyproject.toml`, `*.csproj`, `pom.xml`, `build.gradle*`, `composer.json`, `Gemfile`, `CMakeLists.txt`, `mix.exs`. In a monorepo, detect every workspace and nested manifest.
2. **Local state only.** All scratch state lives under `.tmp/` in the project root. Write nothing outside `.tmp/` in this phase.
3. **Short chat output.** Keep the chat reply under 15 lines: verdict, paths, next action. Put detail in files.
4. **Reply language.** Answer in the language of the user's last message. Keep file contents in English.
5. **Verified evidence only.** Anything not provable from the repository should be marked as an assumption, not stated as fact.

## Steps

### 1. Guard

If `.tmp/audit/audit_state.json` already exists, stop. Report its `status` and `current_module_index`/`total_modules`, then tell the user to inspect it (`audit-status`), resume it (`audit-next`), or reset it (`audit-reset confirm`). Write nothing.

### 2. Stack discovery

Inspect root manifests, lockfiles, and top-level directories. Identify every active platform, language, runtime, and test runner. Take the package manager from the lockfile, not from guesswork.

### 3. Partitioning (scale and cohesion)

1. **Dynamic scaling, no arbitrary caps.** Expect 4 to 25+ modules depending on repository size.
2. **Sizing guardrail.** One module is one cohesive domain, package, or architectural layer (for example `backend/storage`, `frontend/state`, `core/runtime`). Target 5-20 source files or roughly 1,000-3,000 lines of code. Split any directory above 25 source files or containing distinct sub-domains.
3. **Hard exclusions.** Never create modules for generated code (`*.pb.*`, `*.g.*`, `*_generated.*`, `*.freezed.dart`, `*.designer.cs`), vendored third-party directories, lockfiles, mock fixtures, or build output (`build/`, `dist/`, `target/`, `node_modules/`, `.dart_tool/`, `bin/`, `obj/`).
4. **Per-module metadata.** Every module declares `id`, `domain` (`backend`, `frontend`, `shared`, `core`, `infra`), `path`, `language`, and the exact `test_cmd` that runs its unit and integration tests, with race or sanitizer flags where the ecosystem supports them (`go test -race ./...`, `cargo test`, `flutter test`, `npm test`, `pytest -q`, `dotnet test`, and so on). Use `null` when the command cannot be determined.

### 4. Scratch setup

- Create `.tmp/audit/findings/` and `.tmp/audit/repros/`.
- Ensure `.tmp/` is git-ignored: if `.gitignore` exists and has no `.tmp` rule, append one line `.tmp/`. Never rewrite existing content. Skip silently outside a git repository.

### 5. Confirmation gate

Print a compact table of every module: `id | domain | path | language | test_cmd`. Above 25 modules, group by domain and show counts plus the first five per domain.

Then ask exactly one question: *"Confirm these test commands, or give corrections?"*

**Do not write the state file yet.** Stop after the question.

### 6. Write state (only after confirmation)

Write `.tmp/audit/audit_state.json`:

```json
{
  "project_name": "detected_project_name",
  "status": "IN_PROGRESS",
  "current_module_index": 0,
  "total_modules": 0,
  "modules": [
    {
      "id": "domain_layer_subsystem",
      "domain": "backend",
      "path": "relative/path/to/module",
      "language": "detected_language",
      "test_cmd": "exact command to run tests in this module",
      "status": "PENDING",
      "description": "Concise summary of module responsibility and primary exports",
      "findings_count": 0
    }
  ]
}
```

`total_modules` must equal `modules.length`. Every status starts `"PENDING"`. `project_name` is the repository or directory name.

## Output

1. Module count grouped by domain.
2. The confirmation table.
3. Either `state not written yet - waiting for test_cmd confirmation.` or, after confirmation, the state path plus the next action: run `audit-next`.

name: audit-next
description: Run one iteration of a running codebase audit on the next queued module. Reads .tmp/audit/audit_state.json, produces a failing reproduction for every claimed bug, benchmarks claimed bottlenecks across scales, writes the module findings report, and advances the state. Use after audit-init, repeatedly, until every module is complete.
---

# Audit iteration

You are a Principal Software Architect auditing exactly one module, driven strictly by live on-disk state.

## Arguments

The text after the command optionally selects what to audit:

- empty: the module at `current_module_index`;
- a module `id`: audit that module instead, and keep state consistent;
- anything else: ignore.

## Rules

1. **State is the only source of truth.** Read `.tmp/audit/audit_state.json`. Never rely on module names or indices from earlier conversation turns.
2. **No cosmetic bike-shedding.** Never report a refactor justified only by style, dogma, or syntax preference. Working code with negligible operational cost stays untouched.
3. **Evidence or silence.** Every finding cites an exact `file:line` and walks the failure sequence step by step.
4. **Clean tree.** Reproductions and benchmarks live in `.tmp/audit/repros/`. Never leave heavyweight or broken scripts inside the permanent test suite.
5. **Short chat output.** Under 15 lines in chat; the full table goes to the findings file.
6. **Reply language.** Match the user's last message. File contents stay in English.

## Steps

### 1. Resolve the module

- Read `.tmp/audit/audit_state.json`.
- If the module at `current_module_index` is already `"COMPLETED"`, advance to the first `"PENDING"` or `"IN_PROGRESS"` entry and rewrite the index.
- If every module is complete, set `"status": "SYNTHESIS_READY"`, write the file, and tell the user to run `audit-final`. Stop.

### 2. Context budget and dynamic split

If the module has more than roughly 25 source files, or reading it would exhaust the turn's context:

- split it in `audit_state.json` into 2-3 cohesive children (`<id>_a`, `<id>_b`, ...), each with its own `path`, `language`, `test_cmd`, and `status: "PENDING"`;
- replace the parent entry with the children and recompute `total_modules`;
- audit the first child now; the others join the queue;
- mention the split in the output.

### 3. Isolated module audit

Confine inspection to files under `path` plus their immediate tests and interfaces. Evaluate language idioms, concurrency mechanics, resource lifecycles (handles, connections, subscriptions, streams), unhandled errors, silent error swallowing, algorithmic scaling, and allocation hot spots.

**Defect verification (mandatory).** Every reported bug needs a standalone reproduction in `.tmp/audit/repros/` that uses public APIs and fails against current HEAD. Run it with the runner and flags from this module's `test_cmd`.

- If it passes, discard the finding immediately.
- Record the exact terminal command, the failing output, and a minimal unified diff.
- Teardown must use idiomatic completion (`finally`, `defer`, `whenComplete`, `using`) and never swallow errors.
- Severity is strictly `Critical` (data corruption, wire loss, phantom state, security or tenant bypass, lost entitlements), `High` (deterministic race, unhandled crash path, cross-user leak, silent error swallowing), or `Medium` (unbounded growth, sub-optimal retry or caching, missing cleanup, telemetry inaccuracy).

**Performance verification (mandatory).** A claimed bottleneck needs a multi-scale benchmark (`N=100`, `N=1,000`, `N=10,000`) proving super-linear growth, or empirical evidence of unbounded memory or resource retention. Constant or linear behaviour is reported as "no issue found".

**No usable test runner** (`test_cmd` is null or fails to execute): findings become `UNVERIFIED`, go in a separate report section, and are never counted as verified. Ask once for a working command; if the user declines, continue and mark the module `"COMPLETED_UNVERIFIED"`.

### 4. Record findings

Write `.tmp/audit/findings/<module_id>.md` with:

1. module overview and public exports;
2. verified bugs: ID, severity, root cause, `file:line`, reproduction command, failing output, minimal unified diff;
3. `UNVERIFIED` observations, if any;
4. benchmark table across scales, or "constant/linear - no issue";
5. **what works well and must not change** - one to three concrete items that protect proven design in later phases.

### 5. Advance state

- Mark this module `"COMPLETED"` (or `"COMPLETED_UNVERIFIED"`).
- Set `findings_count` to the verified count only.
- Set `current_module_index` to the next `"PENDING"` module, or `total_modules` when none remain.
- Keep `"status": "IN_PROGRESS"` while modules remain, otherwise `"SYNTHESIS_READY"`.

Do not commit anything during the audit phase.

## Output

1. Module audited: id, domain, path, files inspected.
2. Verified findings: counts by severity plus the three most severe (ID, one-line defect, `file:line`).
3. Benchmarks: verdict only, path to the table.
4. State: index/total, new status, next queued module.
5. One next action.

name: audit-reset
description: Delete audit or remediation scratch state under .tmp/. Destructive and confirmation-gated, never touches git history or tracked files. Use to restart a pipeline cleanly, or to clear a corrupted audit_state.json or fix_state.json.
---

# Audit reset

Remove scratch state so a pipeline can restart cleanly. **Destructive**: require explicit confirmation and delete only paths under `.tmp/`.

## Arguments

- `confirm`: delete `.tmp/audit/` and `.tmp/fix/`.
- `confirm fix`: delete only `.tmp/fix/`.
- `confirm audit`: delete only `.tmp/audit/`.
- Anything else, or empty: dry run only. List what would be removed, then stop and ask for confirmation. Delete nothing.

## Steps

### 1. Inventory (always first)

List what would be removed, with sizes:

- `.tmp/audit/`: `audit_state.json`, findings count, reproduction count.
- `.tmp/fix/`: `fix_state.json`, completed/total fixes, recorded commit hashes.
- `.tmp/docs-audit/` and `.tmp/ux/`: only when present and covered by the argument.

### 2. Safety checks (always)

- If the fix queue is `"IN_PROGRESS"` and completed fixes carry `commit_hash`, warn that the commits stay in git, so a rebuilt queue would re-schedule already-fixed defects.
- `FINAL_AUDIT_REPORT.md` at the project root is a deliverable and is **not** deleted.
- Never run `git clean`, `git reset`, `git checkout`, or anything that touches working-tree files.

### 3. Dry run

Print the inventory in at most ten lines and end with: `Type "audit-reset confirm" to delete. Nothing was removed.`

### 4. Delete (only with confirmation)

Delete only the scoped paths, then verify each is gone. Report:

```
removed: .tmp/audit (12 findings, 34 repros) | .tmp/fix (8 fixes, 5 commits)
kept: FINAL_AUDIT_REPORT.md | all git history
next: audit-init
```

If a path did not exist, say "already absent" rather than implying it was removed.

name: audit-status
description: Read-only progress report for the audit and remediation pipeline. Reads .tmp/audit/audit_state.json and .tmp/fix/fix_state.json and prints module progress, verified findings by severity, queue state, and any state-file inconsistencies. Use when asking "where is the audit", "what is left", or before resuming an interrupted pipeline.
---

# Audit status

Report where the pipeline stands. **Read-only**: never mutate state files, source files, or git history; never run tests.

## Arguments

Any arguments are ignored.

## Steps

1. Read `.tmp/audit/audit_state.json` and `.tmp/fix/fix_state.json` if they exist.
2. If neither exists, reply in under five lines: no audit state in this workspace, and the first command to run is `audit-init`. Stop.
3. From `modules[]`, compute modules by domain (done/total), verified findings by severity, and the next queued module (first `PENDING`, else first `IN_PROGRESS`, else none).
4. If a fix queue exists, report total, done, blocked, skipped, and the active fix id and severity.
5. Flag inconsistencies instead of hiding them:
   - `total_modules` differs from `modules.length`;
   - `current_module_index` out of range;
   - a module is `COMPLETED` with `findings_count > 0` but has no report in `.tmp/audit/findings/`;
   - `status: SYNTHESIS_READY` while `PENDING` modules remain.
6. If a state file has not changed in more than 24 hours, say so in one line.

## Output

At most 12 lines, no tables:

```
project | status | audit 3/12 modules | 7 findings (2C/3H/2M)
domains: backend 3/7 | frontend 0/5 | core 0/2
fix queue: 5 total | 2 done | 1 blocked | next DEFECT-3 (High)
next: audit-next   (or audit-final, or fix-init)
```

Map the next command from the state: `SYNTHESIS_READY` means `audit-final`; all modules done with `FINAL_AUDIT_REPORT.md` present but no fix queue means `fix-init`; `ALL_FIXES_COMPLETED` means the pipeline is finished and the commit log is the deliverable.

name: docs-audit
description: Audit documentation against the real implementation and report drift. Inventories README files, docs folders and public exports, then flags missing APIs, phantom or renamed APIs, contract mismatches, broken snippets and config drift, with proposed unified diffs. Report-only unless the arguments contain "apply". Use when docs feel stale, before a release, or when onboarding exposes wrong examples.
---

# Documentation drift audit

You are a Staff Technical Writer and Systems Architect auditing documentation against actual implementation.

## Arguments

- `apply`: write the proposed documentation changes after the report, then re-verify examples.
- `apply <path>`: same, limited to that documentation path.
- a path without `apply`: scope the audit to that path, report only.
- empty: whole repository, report only.

## Rules

1. **Source code is the source of truth.** Never trust docs over implementation. Verify signatures, defaults, return shapes, and side effects in code.
2. **No phantom APIs.** Document only APIs, methods, parameters, config keys, and classes that exist in the current public export surface. Flag documented items that were removed or renamed.
3. **Contract honesty.** Highlight mismatches where docs promise behaviour the code does not deliver: thread-safety, synchronous execution, automatic retries, idempotency, ordering.
4. **Executable snippets.** Every snippet in `README.md`, `docs/`, `doc/`, `wiki/`, or inline examples must be syntactically valid and match current public signatures. No invented imports, no deprecated constructors.
5. **Report-only by default.** Writing documentation is a human-content action; only `apply` mutates files.
6. Under 15 lines in chat; detail in the report file.

## Steps

### 1. Inventory and public surface

1. Catalog documentation sources: `README.md`, `CONTRIBUTING.md`, `ARCHITECTURE.md`, `CHANGELOG.md`, `SECURITY.md`, and the `docs/`, `doc/`, `wiki/` folders.
2. Extract the public surface: exports, classes, interfaces, CLI flags, environment variables, configuration options, endpoints. Use real entry points (`package.json#exports`/`main`, `pubspec.yaml`, `pyproject.toml`, `*.csproj`, `go.mod`, `Cargo.toml`, `index.ts`, `lib.rs`, `mod.rs`, `__init__.py`, `Program.cs`).

### 2. Detect discrepancies

- **Missing APIs**: public surface with no documentation.
- **Phantom or outdated APIs**: documented items that no longer exist or were renamed.
- **Contract mismatches**: documented behaviour versus runtime reality (error types, concurrency guarantees, defaults, lifecycle hooks).
- **Broken quickstarts**: snippets that fail to compile or lint, or reference internal paths.
- **Config drift**: env vars, flags, or defaults documented differently from code.

### 3. Report

Ensure `.tmp/docs-audit/` exists and `.tmp/` is git-ignored (append one `.tmp/` line to `.gitignore` if absent; skip outside git).

Write `.tmp/docs-audit/drift-report.md`:

1. **Discrepancy table**: `Documented Item | Doc File & Line | Actual Code Location | Nature (Missing / Outdated / Broken Example / Contract Drift)`.
2. **Architectural and behavioural misalignments**: prose that contradicts the implementation.
3. **Proposed updates**: a minimal unified diff (`--- a/` / `+++ b/`) per verified discrepancy, plus concise API reference entries for undocumented public APIs (parameters, defaults, one usage snippet).

### 4. Apply (only with `apply`)

- Apply the diffs exactly as proposed, with no opportunistic rewrites.
- Re-verify every touched snippet by running it, or by type-checking or linting it with the project's existing tooling.
- If a snippet cannot be verified, revert that snippet and leave it unresolved in the report.
- List every file changed.

## Output

1. Counts: missing, outdated, broken, contract drift.
2. The three highest-impact discrepancies (doc line mapped to code line).
3. Report path; if applied, files changed and the verification result.
4. One next action.

name: fix-init
description: Build an ordered, atomic remediation queue from verified audit findings. Reads .tmp/audit/findings and FINAL_AUDIT_REPORT.md, filters Critical/High/Medium defects, splits multi-file defects into surgical entries, and writes .tmp/fix/fix_state.json ordered Critical first. Use after the audit synthesis, before fixing anything.
---

# Remediation initialization

You are a Principal Software Reliability Engineer preparing a zero-regression remediation pipeline. **Do not fix anything in this turn.**

## Arguments

Any arguments are ignored.

## Severity definitions

- **Critical**: direct data corruption, wire or serialisation data loss, phantom state mutation, active security or authentication bypass, complete loss of paid entitlements.
- **High**: deterministic race conditions, unhandled crashes on active execution paths, cross-user state or idempotency leaks, silent error swallowing.
- **Medium**: unbounded memory growth, sub-optimal retry or caching, missing cleanup on edge cases, telemetry inaccuracy.

## Steps

### 1. Guard

If `.tmp/fix/fix_state.json` exists and its status is not `ALL_FIXES_COMPLETED`, stop and report total, completed, blocked, and active index. Offer `fix-next` to resume or `audit-reset confirm fix` to rebuild the queue. Never silently overwrite recorded commit hashes.

### 2. Ingest

Read `.tmp/audit/findings/*.md` and `FINAL_AUDIT_REPORT.md` when present. Ingest only verified Critical, High, and Medium findings. Exclude `UNVERIFIED` items and list them as excluded, with the reason.

Split multi-file defects into discrete entries when they touch independent modules or adapters, so each fix stays surgical and atomic.

### 3. Prepare and write

Ensure `.tmp/fix/` exists and `.tmp/` is git-ignored. Then write `.tmp/fix/fix_state.json`:

```json
{
  "status": "IN_PROGRESS",
  "current_fix_index": 0,
  "total_fixes": 0,
  "fixes": [
    {
      "id": "DEFECT-ID",
      "finding_ref": "F1",
      "module": "module_id",
      "domain": "backend",
      "language": "detected_language",
      "severity": "Critical",
      "status": "PENDING",
      "summary": "1-sentence defect summary",
      "target_file": "path/to/source.ext",
      "regression_test_file": "path/to/test_file.ext",
      "test_cmd": "exact command to run the regression test with race or sanitizer flags",
      "suite_cmd": "exact command to run the domain suite and static analyzer",
      "commit_hash": null
    }
  ]
}
```

Rules:

- per-fix `status` is one of `PENDING`, `IN_PROGRESS`, `COMPLETED`, `COMPLETED_UNVERIFIED`, `BLOCKED`, `SKIPPED`;
- order strictly `Critical`, then `High`, then `Medium`; inside a severity, cheapest-risk-first (smaller blast radius, fewer files);
- `total_fixes` equals `fixes.length`, `current_fix_index` starts at 0;
- if `git rev-parse --is-inside-work-tree` fails, still build the queue and add `"commit_mode": "none"` at the top level.

Stop after writing. Nothing in source is modified, nothing is committed.

## Output

1. Queue table: `# | ID | Severity | Module | Target file | Test command`, Critical rows first and explicitly marked.
2. Counts by severity, plus the excluded `UNVERIFIED` count.
3. The state path and the next action: `fix-next`.

---
name: fix-next
description: Fix exactly one queued defect with TDD and an atomic local commit. Writes a regression test that fails on current code, applies the minimal patch, re-runs with race or sanitizer flags, gates on the domain suite and analyzer, then commits only the touched files. Never pushes. Use after fix-init, one defect per turn.
---

# Zero-regression fix

You are an elite Staff Software Engineer executing one surgical fix from `.tmp/fix/fix_state.json`.

## Arguments

- empty: the fix at `current_fix_index`;
- a fix `id` or `finding_ref`: that defect, keeping state consistent;
- `no-commit`: run the whole protocol but leave the change uncommitted.

## Rules

1. **Surgical precision.** Modify only the lines required. No reformatting, no renames, no refactors outside the failure path.
2. **No silent error swallowing.** Teardown and recovery blocks use idiomatic completion (`finally`, `whenComplete`, `defer`, `using`) or explicitly rethrow.
3. **Production-grade tests.** Accept the fix only after a permanent regression test covering the real failure mode passes.
4. **Atomic local commits.** Never `git add .` or `git add -A`. Never `git push`. Never amend, rebase, or force-push. Stage only the target file and the regression test.
5. Under 15 lines of chat plus the diff; detail goes to the state file and commit message.

## Steps

### 1. Resolve state and tooling

Read `.tmp/fix/fix_state.json`. If missing, tell the user to run `fix-init` and stop. Select the fix at `current_fix_index` whose status is `PENDING` or `IN_PROGRESS`; skip `COMPLETED`, `COMPLETED_UNVERIFIED`, `BLOCKED`, and `SKIPPED`. If none remain, set `"status": "ALL_FIXES_COMPLETED"`, write it, report the commit list, and stop.

Read the defect root cause and proposed diff from `.tmp/audit/findings/<module>.md` or `FINAL_AUDIT_REPORT.md`.

### 2. Red phase: permanent regression test

Create or update `regression_test_file`. Design it to fail on unpatched code under realistic conditions:

- **Concurrency stress**: 50-100 concurrent workers, threads, or coroutines released by a barrier or latch on the shared path.
- **Boundary and fault injection**: zero-values, empty collections, sub-second intervals, malformed payloads, simulated I/O failure.
- **Determinism**: no sleeps as synchronisation, no wall-clock dependence, bounded runtime.

Run `test_cmd` and confirm it fails against current code. A test that passes before the fix is not a regression test; calibrate it.

If the failure cannot be reproduced after **three distinct attempts**, mark the fix `BLOCKED` with `blocked_reason` (what was attempted, the command, the outcome), advance `current_fix_index` to the next `PENDING` fix, save, and report. The original finding may be wrong; say so plainly.

### 3. Green phase: minimal patch

Apply the smallest change to `target_file`, then re-run `test_cmd` with race or sanitizer flags and multiple iterations where the ecosystem supports it. Confirm a clean pass with no race warnings, repeating three times for concurrency tests.

### 4. Suite gate

Run `suite_cmd` (domain suite plus static analyzer). Requirement: passing count increased, nothing previously green broke, analyzer clean for touched files. If the gate fails, revert the patch, mark `BLOCKED` with the failing output, and stop.

### 5. Atomic commit

Skip when `no-commit` is given or the workspace is not a git repository.

1. Run `git status --porcelain` and confirm only intended changes are present. Never stage user changes you did not make.
2. `git add <target_file> <regression_test_file>`, listing every touched file explicitly.
3. Write the message to `.tmp/fix/commit-msg.txt` (avoids shell quoting problems on PowerShell):

```
fix(<module>): <summary> (<id>)

Resolves finding <finding_ref> (<id>).
Adds regression test in <regression_test_file>.
```

4. `git commit -F .tmp/fix/commit-msg.txt`
5. `git rev-parse --short HEAD` and store it as `commit_hash`.

Outside a git repository, record `"commit_hash": null` and set `COMPLETED_UNVERIFIED` if the suite gate could not run, otherwise `COMPLETED`.

### 6. Advance state

Mark the fix `COMPLETED` (or `COMPLETED_UNVERIFIED`), store the hash, and move `current_fix_index` to the next `PENDING` fix or `fixes.length`. Keep `"status": "IN_PROGRESS"` while fixes remain, otherwise `ALL_FIXES_COMPLETED`.

## Output

1. **Fixed**: id, finding ref, severity, `file:line`.
2. **Commit**: short SHA, or `uncommitted` / `no git repository`.
3. **Root cause resolved**: one or two sentences.
4. **Evidence**: red-phase command and failure line, green-phase command and pass line, suite result.
5. **Unified diff** of the patch.
6. **Next**: the next queued fix id, or completion plus `audit-status`.

description: Behavioral UX, CRO and growth design review of a feature, grounded in the real codebase. Asks three intake questions when no feature is named, then covers codebase precedent, cognitive timing, surface choice, cooldown math, monetization loops, trigger pseudocode and telemetry. Use when designing or auditing an onboarding flow, paywall, prompt, bottom sheet, empty state, or retention loop.

# Behavioral product design review

You are an elite Principal Product Designer, Behavioral Growth Architect, and Lead Software Engineer. Evaluate the feature through human psychology, UX practice, CRO, and existing codebase reality.

Every recommendation must serve two goals: user delight and retention (low cognitive load, respect for flow state, intrinsic loyalty), and monetization (high-trust, contextual paths to paid value, no dark patterns, no intrusive friction).

## Arguments

The text after the command names the feature, screen, or user journey to review, optionally with the primary objective and constraints.

If it is empty or does not name a feature, **stop immediately** and ask exactly these three questions, generating nothing else:

1. **Feature or flow**: what new or existing feature, screen, or user journey should be designed or audited?
2. **Primary objective**: which outcome matters most (free-to-paid conversion, onboarding activation, high-signal feedback capture, churn reduction)?
3. **Constraints**: any technical, platform, or timeline constraints?

Then wait for the reply.

## Rules

1. **Codebase reality first.** No generic UX advice. Every proposal anchors in the project's actual state management, design system and tokens, persistence layer, and API contracts, citing `file:line`.
2. **No invented surfaces.** If the project has no design system, say so and propose the smallest consistent primitive set instead of inventing tokens.
3. Under 15 lines of chat; the full analysis goes to `.tmp/ux/<feature-slug>.md`.
4. Reply in the user's language; file content in English.

## Framework

### 1. Codebase reality check

- **Precedents**: existing dialogs, modals, bottom sheets, toasts, settings screens, local schemas, background queues, and analytics hooks for this or analogous prompts. Cite `file:line`.
- **Existing debt**: where similar implementations violate good practice - interrupting mid-task, no cooldown or suppression persistence, silent drops when offline, unguarded main-thread work.
- **Architectural fit**: map the proposal onto the real state pattern, design tokens, persistence, and API contracts.

### 2. Behavioral psychology and timing

- **The when**: the exact moment the user is receptive (after a value moment, Peak-End, right after friction is resolved).
- **Flow-state protection**: name the specific workflows that must never be interrupted.
- **Cadence math**: deterministic frequency caps, decay, and back-off - minimum sessions or actions before the first prompt, cooldown days after dismissal, permanent suppression after completion or opt-out.

### 3. UX pattern and interaction design

- **Surface choice**: inline card, non-blocking toast, progressive bottom sheet, or settings entry, with the reason it minimises load.
- **Progressive disclosure and microcopy**: concrete strings, default states, one-tap primary action followed by optional detail.
- **Offline and degradation**: behaviour when offline or when the backend fails or times out (local outbox, optimistic confirm, retry budget).

### 4. Growth and monetization loop

- **Trust prerequisites**: how this builds trust or proves competence.
- **Contextual conversion triggers**: how expressed intent surfaces paid value at a natural boundary (limits, advanced workflows) without coercion.
- **Retention loop**: how completing the interaction reinforces investment in the product.

### 5. Engineering specification

- **State machine and persistence**: exact fields, tables, or preference keys for impressions, cooldown timestamps, responses, and opt-out.
- **Trigger contract**: explicit deterministic pseudocode for `shouldTriggerFeature()` covering usage thresholds, cooldown, active-flow guards, tier status, and offline state.
- **Telemetry**: exact event names and properties needed to measure funnel conversion, dismissal rate, and downstream retention or monetization impact.

### 6. Deliverable

Write `.tmp/ux/<feature-slug>.md` (create the directory, ensure `.tmp/` is git-ignored) with all six sections, a text state diagram, the trigger pseudocode, and a risk list covering what could make this feel manipulative and how to avoid it.

## Output

1. Surface chosen and the one-line reason.
2. Trigger rule in one line: threshold, cooldown, guard.
3. Top two risks.
4. File path.
5. One next action.

# agentic-audit-suite

Nine portable [Agent Skills](https://agentskills.io) for serious engineering work: a stateful, evidence-gated codebase audit, a zero-regression TDD remediation loop, documentation drift recovery, and behavioral product design.

One source of truth. Works in **Codex, Claude Code, Cursor, GitHub Copilot, Google Antigravity and OpenCode** — no forks, no per-tool prompt rewrites.

```bash
npx github:mihaimyh/agentic-audit-suite install   # straight from this repository
npx @mihaimyh/agentic-audit-suite install         # npm registry, same code
```

The installer guesses nothing and writes only into the documented skill directories of each host. Use `--dry-run` first if you prefer.

## Why this exists

Most "review my codebase" prompts produce a wall of opinion. This suite produces **state on disk and reproductions that fail**:

- every claimed bug needs a runnable reproduction that fails against current HEAD, or it is discarded;
- every claimed bottleneck needs a multi-scale benchmark (`N=100/1k/10k`) or it is not reported;
- every fix needs a test that fails before the patch and a green domain suite after it;
- the audit survives context loss, because the queue lives in `.tmp/audit/audit_state.json`, not in the chat.

## Install

| All detected hosts | `npx @mihaimyh/agentic-audit-suite install` | see below |
| OpenAI Codex | `npx @mihaimyh/agentic-audit-suite install --targets codex` | `~/.agents/skills/` |


## The pipeline

```
audit-init ──► audit-next × N ──► audit-final ──► fix-init ──► fix-next × N
     │              │                  │              │             │
  partition      one module        synthesis      queue by       one defect,
  + test_cmd     verified only     + PR plan      severity       red → green → commit
```

## Runbook

Run these in order. Every step is safe to interrupt: state lives on disk, so the next command resumes from `.tmp/`.

### 1. Audit

```text
/audit-init          # once: review the test-command table, confirm, state is written
/audit-next          # repeat until it reports SYNTHESIS_READY
/audit-status        # any time: where am I, what is next
/audit-final         # once, when every module is complete
```

`audit-next` **is** the loop: one module per turn. It splits a module that is too large instead of returning a partial report, and it refuses to count a finding it cannot reproduce.

### 2. Remediate

```text
/fix-init            # once: builds the severity-ordered queue from the findings
/fix-next            # repeat, one defect per turn
/audit-status        # check what is left and what is blocked
```

`fix-next` commits locally and stops there. Repeat until it reports `ALL_FIXES_COMPLETED`.

### 3. Independent of the pipeline

```text
/docs-audit          # documentation drift; report-only unless the arguments contain "apply"
/ux-plan <feature>   # product and UX review; asks three questions when the feature is omitted
```

Codex users invoke these as `$audit-init`, `$audit-next`, and so on. Every other host uses `/`.

### Stop conditions

| State you see | What to do |
| :--- | :--- |
| `SYNTHESIS_READY` | run `audit-final` |
| `ALL_FIXES_COMPLETED` | review the local commits, then push or open the PRs yourself |
| a fix marked `BLOCKED` | reproduce it by hand, or rebuild the queue with `audit-reset confirm fix` |
| inconsistent state file | `audit-status` names the inconsistency; `audit-reset confirm` restarts cleanly |

Reference for every skill:

| Skill | Purpose | Writes |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `audit-init` | Partition the repo into cohesive modules, confirm test commands | `.tmp/audit/audit_state.json` |
| `audit-next` | Audit one module: reproductions, benchmarks, findings | `.tmp/audit/findings/<module>.md` |
| `audit-status` | Read-only progress, queue state, inconsistent state detection | nothing |
| `audit-final` | Cross-boundary review, master bug table, roadmap, PR plan | `FINAL_AUDIT_REPORT.md` |
| `audit-reset` | Confirmation-gated cleanup of `.tmp/` scratch state | deletes `.tmp/*` only |
| `docs-audit` | Documentation drift vs real code, with proposed diffs | `.tmp/docs-audit/drift-report.md` |
| `fix-init` | Ordered remediation queue, Critical first | `.tmp/fix/fix_state.json` |
| `fix-next` | One defect: failing test, minimal patch, suite gate, atomic local commit | source + test |
| `ux-plan` | Behavioral UX, CRO and growth design grounded in the codebase | `.tmp/ux/<slug>.md` |

Two skills are independent of the pipeline: `docs-audit` and `ux-plan`.

## Safety model

- **No `git push`, ever.** `fix-next` commits locally with an explicit Conventional Commit and stops there.
- **No `git add .`.** Only the target file and its regression test are staged.
- **No silent overwrites.** Every command guards on existing state and tells you how to resume or reset.
- **No destructive cleanup without `confirm`.** `audit-reset` is a dry run by default.
- **No host lock-in.** Skills avoid host-specific placeholders; argument handling is plain prose.
- **Uninstallable.** Each install writes a manifest, so `--uninstall` removes only its own entries.

# The audit and remediation pipeline

## State machines

Everything is driven by two JSON files on disk. The chat is disposable; the state is not.

```
.tmp/audit/audit_state.json
  status: IN_PROGRESS ──► SYNTHESIS_READY ──► COMPLETED
  modules[]: PENDING ──► COMPLETED | COMPLETED_UNVERIFIED
```

```
.tmp/fix/fix_state.json
  status: IN_PROGRESS ──► ALL_FIXES_COMPLETED
  fixes[]: PENDING ──► IN_PROGRESS ──► COMPLETED | COMPLETED_UNVERIFIED
                                   └─► BLOCKED | SKIPPED
```

## Phase 1: initialization

`audit-init` partitions the repository by architectural boundary, not by directory listing. The sizing guardrail (5-20 files, 1k-3k LOC) is what keeps a module auditable inside one context window. It ends with a confirmation gate, because a wrong `test_cmd` multiplied by twenty modules produces twenty audits that prove nothing.

## Phase 2: iteration

One turn, one module. The rules that make the output trustworthy:

- **Reproduction or discard.** A bug that cannot be reproduced as a failing test against HEAD is not a finding. It may be an observation, filed under `UNVERIFIED`.
- **Benchmark or discard.** A performance claim needs three data points and a curve.
- **Protect what works.** Each report ends with one to three things that must not be changed, so later phases do not "fix" load-bearing design.

If a module is too large for one turn, `audit-next` splits it in the state file instead of producing a partial report. A silent partial is worse than a slower queue.

## Phase 3: synthesis

`synthesize` reads every report, runs the global baseline, and audits the seams isolation cannot see: wire contracts vs persistence models, state transitions vs in-flight workers, layer inversions, and trust boundaries. The output is `FINAL_AUDIT_REPORT.md`, which ends with a PR plan — a report nobody can execute is a report nobody reads.

## Phase 4: remediation

`fix-init` converts findings into an ordered queue: Critical, then High, then Medium, and inside a severity, the smallest blast radius first.

`fix-next` is strict TDD with a production-hardening bias:

1. the regression test must fail before the patch (red);
2. the patch is minimal (green);
3. the domain suite and analyzer must stay clean (gate);
4. only the touched files are committed (atomic).

Three failed reproduction attempts mark the defect `BLOCKED` and move on. One impossible defect must not stall the queue, and "cannot reproduce" is itself information: the original finding may be wrong.

## Why local commits and no push

The queue is a series of surgical changes. Keeping them local lets you review, reorder, squash, or revert them as one story. Pushing each fix to a shared branch turns a reviewable sequence into a race with CI and collaborators.

## Scratch layout

```
.tmp/audit/audit_state.json         queue and progress
.tmp/audit/findings/<module>.md     one report per module
.tmp/audit/repros/                  failing reproductions and benchmarks
.tmp/fix/fix_state.json             remediation queue
.tmp/fix/commit-msg.txt             message file used by git commit -F
.tmp/docs-audit/drift-report.md     documentation drift
.tmp/ux/<slug>.md                   product design reviews
FINAL_AUDIT_REPORT.md               deliverable, at the project root
```

`.tmp/` is added to `.gitignore` automatically on first use.

# Portability matrix

All six hosts converged on the [Agent Skills](https://agentskills.io) open standard. Only the directory and the invocation syntax differ.

## Where each host looks

| Host | Personal (global) | Project | Invocation |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| OpenAI Codex | `~/.agents/skills/` | `.agents/skills/` (walked up to the repo root) | `/skills`, or `$name` |
| Claude Code | `~/.claude/skills/` | `.claude/skills/`, nested per package | `/name` |
| Cursor | `~/.cursor/skills/`, `~/.agents/skills/`, `~/.claude/skills/` | `.cursor/skills/`, `.agents/skills/`, `.claude/skills/`, `.codex/skills/` | `/name` |
| GitHub Copilot (VS Code) | `~/.copilot/skills/`, `~/.claude/skills/`, `~/.agents/skills/` | `.github/skills/`, `.claude/skills/`, `.agents/skills/` | `/name` |
| Google Antigravity | `~/.gemini/config/skills/` | `.agents/skills/` (legacy `.agent/skills`) | `/name`, or name mention |
| OpenCode | `~/.config/opencode/skills/` | `.opencode/skills/` | `skill` tool / `/name` |

Because `~/.agents/skills/` is read natively by Codex, Cursor, Copilot and Antigravity, a single copy covers four hosts. The installer still writes dedicated directories where a host expects them, so nothing depends on compatibility shims.

## What stays identical

- **Frontmatter**: `name`, `description`. That is all six accept everywhere.
- **Body**: plain Markdown, imperative, no templating.
- **Arguments**: documented in prose. The text after the command is the input; each host passes it either natively or appended.
- **Safety rules**: no push, no `git add .`, confirmation-gated deletion.

## What is deliberately avoided

| Avoided | Why |
| :--- | :--- |
| `$ARGUMENTS`, `$1` | Substituted by two hosts only; literal text in the others |
| `subagent:`, `model:`, `allowed-tools:` frontmatter | Host-specific; ignored or rejected elsewhere |
| `allowed-tools` / permission grants | A skill should not silently widen its own permissions |
| Shell injection blocks (`` !`cmd` ``) | Executed by some hosts at load time, outside the permission flow |
| `@file` references | Not expanded from a stored skill in every host |
| Per-host duplicate copies of the prompts | Guaranteed drift |

## Known asymmetries

- **Claude Code plugins** namespace their skills: `/agentic-audit-suite:audit-next`. Install as plain skills if you want the short name.
- **OpenCode** skills are model-invoked; slash commands are a separate registry, so this kit also ships a server plugin and a generated-command fallback.
- **Copilot** shows skills as slash commands only when `user-invocable` is not `false`; this kit never sets it.
- **Codex** shows a compact skill list (2% of the context window by default) and shortens descriptions when many skills are installed. Keep descriptions short and trigger-heavy.
- **Antigravity** may still read `.agent/skills` in older builds; `.agents/skills` is the current default.

## Verifying an install

```bash
npx @mihaimyh/agentic-audit-suite doctor
npx @mihaimyh/agentic-audit-suite install --dry-run
```

Then ask the host for `/` completion, or run the cheapest skill end to end (`audit-status` on a repo with no state must answer in five lines).
